response.passage: To understand geometry, we must look closely at shapes and angles. First, consider angles. An angle is formed by two rays meeting at a common vertex. A common mistake is thinking that longer arms make an angle larger, but the size of an angle depends only on the opening between the arms, not their length. When measuring, you must place the protractor's centre exactly on the vertex, not anywhere else along the arm. If the arms form a perfectly flat path, we call this a straight angle, which measures exactly 180 degrees. Moving to triangles, we classify them by their sides. An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal, regardless of its orientation or which way it points. Similarly, an isosceles triangle has at least two equal sides; if the third side happens to be equal as well, it remains isosceles, though we often call it equilateral. Finally, consider 3D solids like a cube. A cube has faces, edges, and vertices. An edge is strictly a line segment where two faces meet. We do not count corners as edges, nor do we count curved lines as edges on a flat-faced solid. Remember that a square is a special type of rectangle because it satisfies all the properties of a rectangle, including having four right angles.
response.summary: This passage explains how to correctly measure angles and classify triangles regardless of their orientation. It also clarifies the definitions of 3D edges and the relationship between squares and rectangles.
